items.title: The surprising upside of envy, the emotion we’re taught to hide
items.summary: There was a distinct moment when I stopped being a happy-go-lucky little girl, one who could play for hours alone at the bathroom sink with a set of colorful plastic nesting cups, and became someone who felt left behind and unseen. I was six. I woke up early one Saturday morning in 1975 to silence, which meant my parents were still asleep in their makeshift bedroom — what was once the dining room. They had given me the sole bedroom in our small apartment in Evanston, Illinois. To get to them or any food in the kitchen, I had to cross the living room. But something was different. Our living room was full of baby things. There were pastel-colored items everywhere. Stuffed animal toys, baby blankets, clothes, bottles, diapers, pacifiers, a crib, bathtub, shampoos, soaps, and lotion. From the stack of cards on our small dining room table at the other end of the living room, I pieced together that my mother’s friends had thrown her a baby shower. I recalled that she had left to go somewhere the night before. I remembered thinking how strange it was that she was going somewhere at all; she never went out, let alone after a long day of work and the “L” ride back from downtown Chicago. I began to search through the new items. I kept looking, even though deep down, I had a hunch I wouldn’t find what I was looking for. There were no gifts for me. So many toys for the baby. None for me. I had known the baby was coming. Adults asked, “Are you excited to be a big sister?” “Yes!” I answered. “You’re going to make a good big sister!” they said. And I would glow in such praise. But standing in that small living room, I assessed that my unborn sibling had received more possessions in one evening than I had in my entire life. Becoming a big sister was not the main event. The birth of this baby might just change my life. This was my earliest memory of a charged negative emotion. I was full of envy. While we all feel envy, we don’t talk about it. Not only is it unpleasant, but it’s also socially unacceptable. Many consider it a “deadly sin,” and even if you’re not Catholic or Protestant, nearly all religions and cultures see envy as a bad thing. So it’s not surprising that we may want to dismiss it or deny it. Another reason it’s hard to discuss envy is that there is confusion about what it is. We English speakers don’t have a common understanding of it and will use it interchangeably with a similar but different emotion, jealousy. Even experts who study the emotion argue over its definition. Who can blame them? Envy is hard to study because people can’t or won’t talk about it. Sometimes, we’re not fully conscious of it. I use a simple definition: Envy is the negative emotional experience of wanting something that someone else has. You don’t have what you desire, so you feel insufficient; you sense a lack. Seeing it in the possession of the target of your envy, you also feel inferior. It is the combination of lack and less that pains you. Jealousy, on the other hand, requires a third party. It’s the fear of losing an important relationship to a “rival”; you fear the attention or love you have from someone (that you believe is rightfully yours) will go to someone else. Jealousy is a type of envy because what you desire is another person’s affection that a target may possess instead of you. In my story, I envied the toys my unborn brother received at the baby shower. I was also jealous that he received the attention and generosity from relatives and friends that I, as the big sister, did not. Envy is a universal and complex emotion. We all know what it feels like to see someone else have what we want. It can happen whether your colleague gets credit for a win or the big promotion you thought you deserved. But it can also occur throughout the day, like when the drawer pull in your kitchen falls off, again, and you recall your neighbor’s new sleek cabinetry in her kitchen. (To be honest, I’m describing what just happened to me.) Even children, as demonstrated in my story, can experience the ache of deficit and the sting of lowliness. This is why we can find themes of envy in fairy tales, too. Snow White’s beauty ignites the Evil Queen’s wrath upon hearing the mirror tell her she is no longer the “fairest of them all.” We can’t help but envy. All envy begins with a comparison, and we’re wired to compare ourselves to others. It is how humans learned to fit into groups in order to survive. Infants watch adults to pick up on social cues. As social beings, we all look to others to know ourselves and what to desire. Social comparisons also teach us how to advance within organizations, both formal and informal groups that matter to us. This, too, is instinctive, as gaining group status meant better protection and more resources. And so our brains were trained to pay attention to those above us versus those below us on the social ladder. We learn to want what others want. We are drawn to those who have what we desire. It is what anyone with any hint of ambition will do. All envy begins with a comparison, and we’re wired to compare ourselves to others. It is how humans learned to fit into groups in order to survive. Most people think that envy is only about coveting others’ wealth, power, or beauty. There’s a negative connotation suggesting something sinister. This isn’t surprising given how these specific types of envy are shared in Greek tragedies and movie plots. We often neglect, however, that envy can also encompass admiring what others have. We forget the infinite number of other kinds of social ladders that exist. When scientists, athletes, or artists compete, they might feel envy of intellect, skill, or creativity. Even virtues, like spiritual awareness or environmental consciousness, can inspire humans to compare, compete, and hence feel envy. Look at any parenting, health, political, or fitness trend, and you’ll find groups whose members will measure who among them performs their ideals better, is purer, or exemplifies more devotion. We instinctively focus on when we fall short in areas that are important to us. To protect ourselves from harm, our brains have evolved to have what scientists call a “negative bias.” We pay more attention to what’s missing, how we’re behind, and what’s wrong. We take for granted what we have, how well we’re doing, and what’s going right. Despite being natural, it can still be embarrassing to feel inferior or shameful to feel some ill will. Because admitting envy is (currently) unacceptable, we will conceal it or censor ourselves. We may suppress these emotions from percolating to avoid experiencing pain. We learn to do this so fast, we are often not aware of it and therefore can deny feeling it. Other times we may try to quell it by telling ourselves, “Don’t compare yourself with others.” “Run your own race.” “Be thankful for what you have.” Or we may attempt to convince ourselves that having such recognition, wealth, or beauty comes with other heavy burdens. (Sour grapes, anyone?) We will take comfort that we are better in some other way. But I’ve learned something: When we quash, deny, or dismiss our envy, when we don’t discuss or examine it, we miss out on the opportunity to harness it for good. This article The surprising upside of envy, the emotion we’re taught to hide is featured on Big Think .

items.title: How “V for Vendetta” became more than a movie
items.summary: “If we had put some of the stuff that’s happening today into the film back when we were making it, the studio would have told us we were being ridiculous,” James McTeigue, the director of the 2006 film V for Vendetta , tells Big Think. “But V almost seems tame now, a bit like child’s play.” McTeigue sees the film as prophetic: “It was definitely pointing the way to where we ended up.” Few movies leave a legacy as large as V for Vendetta . Although it was met with mixed reviews and modest commercial success upon its release, McTeigue’s adaptation of Alan Moore’s graphic novel of the same name has never truly left the zeitgeist — and there are a couple of reasons. The first has to do with the film’s themes. Moore’s graphic novel — written in the 1980s and illustrated by David Lloyd — attacked the Conservative government of “Iron Lady” Margaret Thatcher. When the film version came out, many viewed it as a critique of Bush-era illiberalism in the wake of 9/11. And with today’s anxieties about mass surveillance, authoritarian tendencies, and national leaders attempting to control media, it’s not hard to see why the film still resonates with audiences two decades after its release. The second reason has to do with the film’s audience and imagery. A testament to the eponymous vigilante’s iconic exclamation that “ideas are bulletproof,” his grinning, mustachioed Guy Fawkes mask has become a popular sight at demonstrations across the globe, from the U.S. and Venezuela to Saudi Arabia and Hong Kong. But how did this happen, and what does it mean? Guy Fawkes Day To understand what the Guy Fawkes mask means to real-world rebels, we first have to understand what it means to V the character. As the film briefly calls upon us to “remember,” Fawkes was executed for his involvement in the 1605 Gunpowder Plot: an unsuccessful attempt by Catholic conspirators to blow up the House of Lords and assassinate the Protestant King James. To commemorate its failure, the day the plot would have taken place — November 5th — was later declared a public holiday. Fawkes, who had been assigned the job of lighting the gunpowder, was not only burned in effigy, but over time, people also started wearing masks that caricatured his distinct appearance. The meaning of this holiday changed. What began as a sober commemoration of a solemn event evolved into a night of bonfires and fireworks, and feelings associated with Fawkes shifted from negative to positive. By the time the Industrial Revolution rolled around — and English Catholics had been officially emancipated — Fawkes was seen less as a villain than as a folk figure. This is also how V seems to see Fawkes. Though the character never really explains why he chose this particular figure as his revolutionary alter ego, his preoccupation with Fawkes’ larger-than-life (and, frankly, different-from-life) reputation rather than the man himself underscores his belief that symbols are more powerful than people. Behind the mask If certain members of Anonymous — the hacking group first credited with adopting the Guy Fawkes mask for real-world demonstrations — are to be believed, V for Vendetta largely owes its political currency to circumstance. Since the hackers decided they would all wear the same kind of mask, they had to pick one that was readily available in stores, and instead of Batman’s, they ended up settling for V’s. (Interestingly, Moore has listed Batman as one of his many, many inspirations for the revolutionary.) The primary purpose of the masks was to provide anonymity . Anonymous is, as the name implies, anonymous. Used to striking from the shadows of the internet, the group took to the streets in February 2008, when thousands of members protested outside Church of Scientology buildings in dozens of cities. Showing up in person put them at risk of identification — a danger, given the church’s history of surveilling and harassing its critics. At the same time, people were not unaware of the masks’ cultural connotations. Thanks to the film, Guy Fawkes was now thoroughly and explicitly linked to revolution, anarchism, and vigilante justice. In the graphic novel, V’s methods and motives are questionable. But on screen, he is presented as a more or less conventional superhero: someone dedicated to fighting the good fight, and turning the world into an unquestionably better place as a result. In short: someone many strive to emulate. If picked for unrelated reasons, the film seemed to inspire the demonstrators. Gathering and posing for photographs, they intentionally mirrored one of the film’s last and most memorable scenes, where ordinary Londoners take up V’s call to action and march across the street wearing his mask: a single force, united behind a single purpose. The power of symbols The masks provide other advantages, too, most of which are likewise explored in the film. For both Anonymous and the Occupy Wall Street movement, which started using them in 2011, they reflect the fact that the demonstrations are decentralized and leaderless, making them difficult to break apart. (Masks obviously also make criminals more difficult to identify, which is why some nations have criminalized wearing masks in certain contexts: Some allow them only in lawful protests, not riots; others ban them during any public protest.) Because symbols are abstract, they can mean different things to different people. “There’s value in abstracting away from what you’re trying to comment on,” McTeigue says. “With the film, we sprinkled enough in there that although the story is set in the U.K., you believe it could happen anywhere.” Although you’d have been more likely to see the Guy Fawkes mask at left-coded protests over the past two decades, it’s not strictly worn by progressives. In the early 2020s, for example, anti-COVID-lockdown protesters in the U.S. and U.K. sometimes wore the mask, as did at least several people at the U.S. Capitol riot on January 6, 2021 . According to one scholarly article on V for Vendetta , the citywide adoption of V’s Guy Fawkes mask is especially powerful because it signifies the people challenging the monopoly on representation held by the state, which the philosopher and political theorist Thomas Hobbes defined as the “sole actor of the body politic.” If image and narrative are two of the primary tools that the film’s fascist government uses to ensure the loyalty (or docility) of its citizenry, then V uses those same tools to dismantle that relationship. Early in the film, he hijacks the state broadcast network to announce a visual spectacle of his own: the destruction of Parliament. In the end, the symbol of government — the building — makes room for the symbol of the people: the masks. How fiction changes the world Popular music, books, films, shows, video games, and other media do not simply reflect society’s problems and aspirations back at itself. According to French historian Patrick Boucheron, who covers this subject in his 2025 book Political Fictions , they also — in a way — predict the future by exploring how those problems and aspirations could play out over time. V for Vendetta is hardly the only piece of pop culture to work its way into real-world demonstrations. Recently, another image of fictional origin — the pirate flag of a Japanese manga and anime franchise called One Piece — became a prominent protest symbol in countries like Indonesia, Nepal, and India. Like the Guy Fawkes mask, the One Piece flag does more than create a feeling of solidarity between protesters. By identifying their own struggles with those of a well-known fictional hero, they not only tap into a narrative that their opponents cannot easily control, but also generate sympathy abroad: anyone familiar with One Piece — the manga alone has sold more than 600 million copies globally — may be predisposed to sympathize with protesters waving the pirate flag, regardless of what the protests are actually about. “All fiction is an escape from

items.title: HUNA Is an Arab Prison Memoir That Refuses to Cater to the Western Gaze
items.summary: In 2013, Abdelrahman ElGendy is a 17-year-old fledgling activist as students like him take to Cairo’s streets in protest against a military coup. Only two years earlier, they’d been swept up in the hope of Egypt’s January 25th revolution. During one mass demonstration, in which Abdelrahman is present as a bystander recording the fervor from his car while his Baba, in the driver’s seat, tells him to put your hand inside , police arrive. They brutally attack protestors and drag Abdelrahman and his Baba away. What follows is a journey from a jail cell to a pre-trial detention center, and then from prison to prison, each step marked by a tug of war with hope as the 15-day sentence renews thrice, extends into a 45-day sentence, which also renews, a trial pending, until the verdict arrives: 15 years of incarceration. Abdelrahman’s debut memoir, Huna , is the devastating, rage-inducing account of this incarceration and the grit and heart needed to not merely survive but claw one’s way out of systemic erasure in post-revolution Egypt. Cloistered between walls and bodies, Abdelrahman learns: First, engineering as part of the bachelors degree he completes; then, how love and guilt can sit in the same room between him and his Baba. He grows: into an inmate who teaches English, Arabic, and more to the young and old; into a young man who looks out for others; a son who watches his mother’s waving hand until it disappears behind the prison gate; and a prisoner seasoned in the lingo of his environment and the politics of survival. In the midst of all of this, Abdelrahman holds onto community, joy, and most of all, tenderness. In conversation, Abdelrahman told me “[Huna] is not a book about how I survived. This is how I survived.” He thinks writing is a militant act, a way to imagine other futures and help others imagine them as well. We spoke about his love for Arabic and the choice to weave it in the memoir, erasure through archival silences, resisting the “soft occupation” of the American empire, and more. Bareerah Ghani: There is a touch of tenderness when you introduce Cairo as Al Qahira. You write that outsiders find the city insufferable but those she had birthed would object. How has your relationship to Cairo, and to Egypt, evolved in the aftermath of your incarceration and exile? How have those experiences shaped the way you think about the blurred lines between a country, its people, and the systems of power that govern them? Abdelrahman ElGendy: I’ve been rereading Avery Gordon’s Ghostly Matters , where she discusses how the ghosts of certain social events and ruptures that are assumed to be of the past still slip into our present and expose its seams and the violent histories that are being suppressed by power. I also think about Christina Sharpe’s In The Wake , where she argues that this myth of a clean break with slavery is sort of a manufactured one; that for Black people, the rupture of enslavement very much structures the present. So when I think of Cairo, of Egypt at large, I think about what it means to live in the wake of the January 25th revolution in 2011 and what ghosts structure modern Egypt. Our military dictatorship blasts us with this mass gaslighting. That what we experienced in the revolution never really happened, and the very present, brutalized population of political prisoners—over 60,000 today, on whose backs this so-called present-day stability rests—are not there. They’re ghosts. And I’m always thinking about how they’re not, actually—they’re on the other side of the wall, but they’re being intentionally ghostified, so to speak. In prison, you think a lot about that idea of erasure and forgetfulness, people just forgetting you exist. You’re ghostified. I think about all the massacres, like the Rabaa Massacre and the massacres of the January 25th Revolution, how they still structure our present in Egypt. And yet, there’s severe repercussions and state repression for anyone who dares question this clean break with the past or invoke the revolution. When the price, not even of action, but just of memory, is so high, it’s sad—and understandable, too—that so many people eventually condition themselves to buy into this myth. It’s more comfortable and safer. So you become sort of complicit in the erasure of our revolutionary past and our bloody, carceral present—not necessarily, again, because you’re evil, but mostly out of a need for survival. For me, on top of it being impossible on a safety level to return to Egypt anymore, it’s also impossible for me to live a life where I am not haunted by these ghosts of what we lost. And also, even more, I guess, by all the ghosts of what could have been in that moment of revolutionary rupture, which was so violently ripped away from us before we were massacred, locked up, or exiled. These ghosts, to me, are the source of both my wistfulness and that tenderness that you mentioned toward Cairo and Egypt. I feel like it’s a curse that will follow me. I will always see these ghosts lurking in every corner of the country as long as I live. BG: In your memoir, you mention Radwa Ashour as a literary influence. She made you ask, “Where do our untold stories go? If they never find an ear, do they cease to exist? Do we ?” I would love for you to talk about that literary awakening while you were amidst a systemic erasure yourself, and how witnessing can be an act of preservation. AEG: In prison, you think a lot about that idea of erasure and forgetfulness, people just forgetting you exist. You’re ghostified. I like to think alongside texts, and with this idea here, I think of Michel-Rolph Trouillot’s Silencing the Past , particularly his idea of archival silences—how silences enter the archive. He speaks a lot about the myth of the factual archive, and how any archive is an act of curation by a curating power that almost always has an agenda. That’s why history is, for the most part, a work of fiction, an approximation of the truth, and sometimes a willful distortion of it that is convenient to power. Archival silences are one of the most lethal tools that power deploys to erase and confine the ghosts of the past it finds inconvenient, and therefore, it suppresses any possibility of the revival of certain histories. And in the process, certain things just become unutterable, even unthinkable, in the present. In the wake of the genocide, writing in English started to feel more complicit than usual. It was etched on the missiles that were bombing Palestinians in Gaza. In prison, it was both fascinating and disturbing to watch the history that led to our incarceration, and our very incarceration, being erased in real time in the state newspapers that we smuggled, or state-sponsored TV shows that our families would tell us about in visitation. At one point, I realized that we were inhabiting an archival silence in the making. That, Oh, it’s not even an archival silence in the past . I’m in it, in real time now . I was seeing it being carved out of the archive, and my body and all our bodies. So this is what I was pointing toward in that line of inquiry, when I ask, Do we cease to exist? I don’t mean only as Egyptians, but also as prisoners, specifically, because prison is in its very function, an institution of invisibilization, of undesirable and inconvenient bodies. I was imagining writing this book in prison specifically for that reason. Among other things, this memoir is my attempt to speak into this archival silence that is being violently ripped out of our history in real time. I want it to be there when anyone reaches for that part of history and wants to relive it, that, specifically inside prisons, they find this project instead of the silence they would’ve found otherwise. So you read this book, and you know that we were there, we struggled, we cried, we broke, we loved, and we found all those ways

items.title: MMX mission to reveal the origins of the Martian moons
items.summary: It was way back in the 1600s — immediately following the invention of the telescope — that moons around planets other than Earth were discovered. Jupiter’s four major moons were spotted by Galileo himself back in 1609 and 1610, leading his contemporary, Johannes Kepler, to hypothesize that the planet in between us and Jupiter — Mars — must have two moons of its own. Yet for centuries, no Martian moons were discovered. The first moons around Saturn were found later in the 17th century, and then Uranus and many of its moons were discovered in the 18th century. Even Neptune and its giant moon, Triton , were discovered back in 1846. Only in 1877 was Kepler’s hunch confirmed : when Asaph Hall spotted Mars’s two tiny satellites for the first time. The larger and innermore of Mars’s two moons, Phobos, is only 22.2 kilometers across, while smaller, more remote Deimos is just 12.6 kilometers wide. Both are very close to the red planet: Phobos completing an orbit every 7.66 hours at a mean distance of 9377 km from Mars’s center, and Deimos completing one every 30.35 hours at a distance of 23,460 km from the center of Mars. Although they’ve been observed remotely many times, these moons have never had an in situ mission dedicated to studying them before, and despite a plethora of indirect evidence, their origins remain uncertain. All of that is poised to change over the next few years, as JAXA’s MMX (Martian Moons eXplorer) mission now heads to Phobos and Deimos, where an orbiter, lander, rover, and sample return mission are all set to teach us more about these remote, tiny worlds than ever before. Here’s what lies in store. The relative sizes of the asteroid-like moons of Mars, Phobos and Deimos. Phobos is the innermost moon of Mars while the smaller Deimos is more than twice as far away. Despite their appearances as looking similar to asteroids, it’s thought that Phobos and Deimos were once joined by a larger, third, inner moon, which has since decayed and fallen back to Mars. All are thought to originate from a giant, ancient impact. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech It might sound like a bit of hyperbole, but when it comes to Mars, understanding its moons is the key to understanding the entire history of the red planet. There are two main scenarios for how these moons came to be, and they would both lead to entirely different planetary histories for Mars, and determining as much as we can about which scenario occurred, and in as much detail as possible, is the whole goal of the MMX mission. The first major scenario for the Martian moons was the one that came along earlier in a chronological sense, and was focused on the size and shape of those moons: that they were captured asteroids. These small, irregular bodies have been discovered to have cratered surfaces, irregular shapes, and low densities: of around 1.8-1.9 g/cm³ for Phobos and around 1.5-1.7 g/cm³ for Deimos, which is comparable to rubble-pile asteroids. The second scenario is more recent, and instead suggests that, much like Earth’s moon, they were formed in the aftermath of a giant impact event. Even though the moons are small, they both orbit in the same plane as the Martian equator, have hints of the reddish color that’s the hallmark of Mars and orbit extremely close in to the red planet, whereas nearly all known captured bodies orbit considerably far out around the worlds that captured them. The possibility that these moons formed from a primordial circumplanetary disk around Mars has also been considered, but for such a small mass planet as Mars, isn’t a particularly viable scenario. Rather than only the two Martian moons we see today, Phobos and Deimos, a collision followed by a circumplanetary disk may have given rise to three moons of Mars, where only two survive today. The idea is that Mars’s once-innermost moon was destroyed and fell back onto Mars long ago. This hypothetical transient moon of Mars, proposed in a 2016 paper, is now the leading idea in the formation of Mars’s moons, and helps explain the enormous differences in topography between Mars’s northern and southern hemispheres. Credit : LabEx UnivEarthS | Université de Paris Diderot For a long time, there was a big problem with the second scenario: simulations of impacts would simply refuse to produce two small moons that were comparable to Phobos and Deimos. If you only produced small moons, they almost always wound up drifting farther away than even Deimos is located, while if you wanted to get multiple moons that were close in, they always wound up being larger. But then, in 2016, a remarkable new scenario was presented , which considered something novel: what if there was an ancient collision that created Phobos and Deimos, but also a third, much larger and more massive moon interior to them both, that has since been destroyed and fallen back onto Mars? All of a sudden, a bunch of puzzle pieces appeared to line up. Mars is one of the most unusual worlds in the Solar System in terms of its geography, with an enormous basin covering approximately half of the planet (the northern hemisphere) and elevated highlands covering the other half (the southern hemisphere), with an elevation difference of about 5 kilometers between the two. There’s one and only one very deep depression in the southern hemisphere, like a large chunk of material caused an ancient impact crater, but it’s the deepest point on the Martian surface by far. The Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) instrument, part of Mars Global Surveyor, collected over 200 million laser altimeter measurements in constructing this topographic map of Mars. The Tharsis region (center-left) is the highest elevation region on the planet, while the lowlands appear in blue. Note the much lower elevation of the northern hemisphere compared to the southern, with a mean difference in elevation of around ~5 km, thought to arise from the fallback of a third, large, former Martian moon. Credit : Mars Global Surveyor MOLA Team We have to keep in mind that the Solar System is old: between 4.5 and 4.6 billion years old, and that Mars has been this way for a very long time, for over 3 billion years at least. However, we are only seeing Mars as it is today; one of the difficulties we have with reconstructing the history of the Solar System is that we are only directly aware of the current survivors. We may have had more planets, moons, impacts, and rings around worlds in the distant past, but that evidence has largely been erased by the passage of time. Today, all that remains is the indirect evidence of their onetime presence, imprinted on whatever worlds, bodies, and features still persist. But there is a surefire way to tell whether the surviving moons of Mars are of asteroidal origin or whether they were formed by an impact that struck Mars: we can determine it the same way we determined that the Moon was formed by a giant ancient impact with Earth, by going there, landing on it, examining what we find, and bringing samples of it back home to analyze and compare it in a laboratory setting. If the material of Phobos and Deimos are different from the material found on Mars, they probably are captured bodies. But if the material is largely identical to the material we find on Mars itself, they’re almost certainly the result of an ancient impact. This close-up image of asteroid Itokawa was taken by the Hayabusa spacecraft in 2005 near its closest approach to the asteroid. Different parts of the asteroid have different densities, indicating that it formed as a contact binary from two predecessor “dirty snowball” asteroids, Itokawa likely has a history where several different smaller objects merged together to form what we see today: a common story among asteroid belt and Kuiper belt objects in our Solar System.
